Part 1 of 3 -- slides 190-198, 6 question(s): shallow_coverage (confidence 0.40)

I examined slides 190‑198 and the matched student questions. The slides list the six primary Linux namespaces and describe their isolation purposes, covering the questions about namespace types, the role of namespaces, PID isolation, MNT isolation, and the lightweight nature of containers. The question about the depth of UTS namespace isolation across nested namespaces is not addressed in these slides. I attempted to expand the context around slide 190 and performed a full‑deck search for "UTS namespace nested depth", but no slide provided that detail. Because the investigation was cut short before a thorough search of all relevant slides, I cannot confirm whether the deck truly omits this information. Thus, I mark this question as having shallow coverage and note that the investigation was incomplete. The overall gap type for the topic is therefore "shallow_coverage".

Part 2 of 3 -- slides 199-209, 8 question(s): covered (confidence 0.90)

The slide set for Topic 14 (slides 199‑209) provides a comprehensive overview that directly addresses each of the eight student questions identified by semantic similarity.  The discussion of containers versus virtual machines explains the reduced overhead of containers in terms of memory, storage, boot time, and I/O, satisfying the question about why containers have less overhead.  The contrast section also clearly delineates the fundamental differences between a container and a VM, covering the second question.  Docker’s role in application portability is explicitly described in the “Docker Improves Application Portability” section, noting how immutable images eliminate the “works on my machine” problem.  The benefits of Docker—portability, fast provisioning, consistent runtime, dependency isolation, and simplified CI/CD—are listed in the “Docker Benefits” portion, answering the fourth question.  The introductory slides define Docker as an open‑platform tool that packages an application and its runtime, directly addressing the fifth question.  The text explicitly states that containers share the host OS kernel, covering the sixth question.  Finally, the “Docker Architecture” slides detail the Docker daemon’s responsibilities and the REST‑API communication between client and daemon, fully answering the last two questions.  No additional context beyond the topic’s slide range is required to answer these queries, so the content is considered fully covered.

Part 3 of 3 -- slides 209-210, 2 question(s): covered (confidence 0.90)

The slides for Topic 14 (209‑210) provide a clear definition of a Docker image and explain that a Dockerfile is a script that specifies the instructions for building an image, with each instruction creating a new layer. This directly answers the question about what a Dockerfile is and what it specifies.

The question about the difference between a Docker image and a Docker container is not addressed in these slides. However, a separate slide (152) in the deck contains a full definition of Docker containers and explains how they are instantiated from images. Since the question is answered elsewhere in the deck, it does not represent a gap for this topic.

Overall, the topic’s slides adequately cover the Dockerfile question, and the container question is answered in a different part of the deck, so the topic is considered covered.
